c1:p0: This is Dickens's preface upon completing the serialization of *David Copperfield*. The author expresses his emotional difficulty in distancing himself from the finished novel, torn between pride in completing his two-year creative endeavor and melancholy at parting with his characters. He acknowledges his reluctance to burden readers with personal feelings about the work's conclusion.
c1:p1: This is the author's postscript to David Copperfield, written in October 1850. Dickens explains that he has nothing additional to add about the story beyond what he has already expressed within the narrative itself, as he is emotionally overwhelmed by completing the two-year writing project and must part with his fictional characters.
c1:p2: This is Dickens's preface to the conclusion of David Copperfield, written in October 1850. The author reflects on the emotional difficulty of completing his two-year serialized novel, expressing the bittersweet feelings of parting with his fictional characters while affirming his deep personal investment in the authenticity of the narrative he has created.
c1:p3: This is the closing passage of Dickens's preface to David Copperfield, written in October 1850. The author reflects on completing the novel after two years of writing and expresses his intention to return to monthly publication of his periodical (likely referring to Household Words), using botanical metaphor to describe his literary endeavors.
c1:p4: This is the author's signature and publication date closing the Preface to David Copperfield, where Dickens reflects on completing his two-year imaginative task and expresses his emotional connection to the characters and narrative he has created.

David Copperfield encounters Uriah Heep on a walk outside Canterbury. After David reveals his engagement to Dora (not Agnes), Uriah responds with a lengthy confessional monologue during their moonlit walk back toward town. In this passage, Uriah explains his philosophy of false humility, revealing how his father taught him that adopting an outward show of humbleness—always deferring to "betters" and knowing one's place—is actually the key to gaining power and advancement. He describes his upbringing at a charitable school where this doctrine of humility was constantly reinforced, and boasts that this strategy has served him well despite its apparent contradiction.
c41:p122: This reflection occurs after Uriah Heep explains how his family was taught false humility from childhood as a survival strategy in their impoverished circumstances. David realizes for the first time that Uriah's characteristic obsequiousness and cant of humility stems from this systematic family conditioning, rather than being innate to his character. The metaphor of "harvest" and "seed" emphasizes David's new understanding of the root cause of Uriah's despicable behavior.
c41:p123: Uriah Heep, during a moonlit walk with David outside Canterbury, reveals the origins of his false humility. He explains how his father taught him to cultivate deliberate humbleness as a strategy for gaining power and advancement, describing how he intentionally limited his own education and adopted servile behavior while secretly accumulating influence over Mr. Wickfield.
c41:p124: David confronts Uriah Heep on a walk outside Canterbury. He reports that the current Mrs. Murdstone has been psychologically broken by her marriage to Mr. Murdstone and his tyrannical sister, describing her deterioration from a lively young woman into a shadow of herself, reduced almost to imbecility by their relentless gloom and austerity.
c61:p131: David has returned to England and is conversing with Mr. Chillip, his childhood doctor, at the Gray's Inn Coffee-house. c61:p133: David Copperfield encounters Mr. Chillip, his childhood doctor, at the Gray's Inn Coffee-house. c61:p134: After returning to England and reuniting with his friend Traddles, David encounters Mr. Chillip, his childhood doctor, at the Gray's Inn Coffee-house. c61:p135: David encounters Mr. Chillip, his childhood doctor, at the Gray's Inn Coffee-house. c63:p38: Copperfield and Traddles visit a prison where their former schoolmaster Creakle now works as a magistrate. Copperfield inquires about the main principles of the prison's solitary confinement system, which Creakle claims achieves prisoner isolation and genuine penitence through this method.

c63:p50: Copperfield and Traddles visit a prison where Mr. Creakle, their former schoolmaster, is now a magistrate.
